title: An integrand with signed shading: what is positive and what is negative area?
summary: The area between a curve and the axis is shaded teal where the function is positive and rose where it is negative. Net area is the signed sum: equal pieces of opposite sign cancel to zero.

media.alt: A sky-blue sine curve from 0 to 2 pi with the region above the axis shaded teal and the region below shaded rose, and a legend naming positive and negative.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: What is positive and negative area?
read_the_figure.axes: x from 0 to 2 pi (6.28). y = f(x) = sin x from -1 to 1. The fill extends from the curve to the line y = 0; teal above, rose below.
look_at: Where does the fill change colour? That is where f changes sign.
Are the teal and rose areas equal? Think about symmetry.
What is the net signed area, and what is the total (unsigned) area?
What does the colour mean: sign of f, not good or bad.
as_drawn: f changes sign at x = pi (3.14). The teal lobe and the rose lobe have the same size.
Net area = integral of sin from 0 to 2 pi = 0. Total area = integral of |sin| = 4 (2 + 2).
The fill is to y = 0, the true baseline for an integral. The legend names colours 'positive' and 'negative'. No numbers are printed.
read_the_figure.proves: The sign structure of the integrand and that equal opposite lobes cancel. It does not prove the lobes are exactly equal: only the integral does.
if_wrong: Fill to a baseline other than zero: shaded area no longer equals the integral.
Colours chosen with no legend: sign cannot be read.
A net-zero result presented as 'no area': the total area (4 here) is hidden.

terms.meaning: The signed area between a curve and the x axis over an interval.
Area counted positive where f > 0 and negative where f < 0.
The integral of the absolute value: both lobes counted positive.
Positive and negative contributions that add to a smaller net value.
A point where f changes sign.
The running integral from a fixed start to x.

remember: Above the axis counts +, below counts -.
Net area is not total area.
Fill to y = 0, never to another baseline.
Name the sign colours in a legend.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The line is the function. The filled regions are area marks bounded by the curve and the zero line; hue encodes sign (teal positive, rose negative) at the same lightness so neither seems 'bigger'. Position carries x and the value of f.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The integral is an accumulation that carries signs, so the right picture shows the sign. Shading makes the sum a visual balance: if one colour is bigger the net is that sign, and if they match the net is zero. The picture also makes the point that a net of zero is not an absence of area.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Area is hard to compare by eye when shapes differ, and aspect ratio changes how big a lobe looks. Net zero can be misread as 'no change' while the total area is large. A colour pair that differs in lightness makes one lobe appear weightier. And the picture shows area in plot units, not physical units.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Sign colours must be fixed (teal positive, rose negative) so the reader never relearns the code. The zero baseline makes the shaded area the actual integral. Both are needed to read the figure as an integral, not as decoration.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the accumulation F(x) in a panel below: it climbs while f is positive and falls while f is negative, ending at the net area. For many lobes use a bar chart of lobe areas. For physical quantities (work, charge) annotate each lobe with its value in units.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the running integral F(x) under the curve, mark F(pi) = 2 and F(2 pi) = 0, and print the net and total areas in the corner.

steps.title: Net and total area of the sine
steps.note: Each lobe has area 2 in magnitude. Numerical integration gives 2e-16 and 4.0000.

steps.title: The accumulation function
steps.note: F rises to its maximum 2 where the integrand crosses zero (x = pi) and then falls back: slope of F is f.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) where does f change sign? (2) What are the net and the total areas? (3) If f were shifted up by 0.5, would the net area change?

solution.text: At x = pi, about 3.14, where the fill switches from teal to rose.
By symmetry the lobes are equal and opposite: net 0, total 4.
Yes: the shifted function has net area 0 + 0.5 x 2 pi = pi, because the shift adds a rectangle of area 0.5 times the width.

worked.answer: Sign change at pi; net 0, total 4; shifting by 0.5 raises the net to pi.

analyze.q: A function has net area 0 over [0, 2 pi] but is not zero. What physical quantity would still be non-zero, such as work?
analyze.hint: Think of a net-zero force over a cycle.

analyze.q: If you fill to y = 0.3 instead of y = 0, what area does the shaded region show?
Where would an error in locating the zero crossing show up in the net area?

evaluate.q: A report quotes 'net area 0.02' for a measured signal that swings strongly. What other numbers should it give?
evaluate.hint: Total area and the size of each lobe.

checks.q: What is the net area of sin x from 0 to 2 pi and why?
checks.answer: Zero: the positive and negative lobes are equal in size and opposite in sign, so they cancel.

checks.q: The total area under |sin x| from 0 to 2 pi?
Why must the fill reach down to y = 0 and not to the bottom of the plot?
checks.answer: The integral is the signed area from the curve to the zero line; a fill to any other baseline adds an unrelated rectangle.
